core_principles.text: Maintain the thigh and foot in line with each other during the squat, keeping the knee approximately aligned with the second toe.
Turn the feet out appropriately based on individual anatomy to open the hips and allow squatting to full depth with an upright posture.
Use the cue 'knees out' combined immediately with 'hips in' when knees cave inward to move the hips forward and restore upright trunk posture.

common_mistakes.text: Actively pushing the knees out beyond the feet when the thighs are already properly aligned with the toes.
Allowing the knees to cave inward as the lifter reaches the sticking point of the squat.

specific_findings.text: Foot turn-out angle required to open the hips and maintain alignment ranges from 5 to 10 degrees for some lifters up to 20 to 30 degrees for others depending on body structure.

consequences.text: Allowing the knees to move inward causes the hips to shift backward, increasing forward trunk lean and placing greater moment loads on the hip and spinal joints.
Increased forward trunk inclination resulting from valgus knee collapse raises the likelihood of the torso collapsing forward and failing the lift.

core_principles.text: Unilateral squat and hinge variations, such as single-leg RDLs, split squats, and lunges, help build global hip stability and control.
Incorporating slow eccentric and pause squats helps lifters develop improved movement control.
Prep or corrective work for knee valgus should focus on the adductors and internal rotators.
Ensure the lifter's stance is proper and that global movement mechanics like posture and bracing are sound when managing knee valgus in a squat.
Corrective work should be implemented to attenuate knee valgus if the inward knee collapse is severe.

common_mistakes.text: Squatting with a mini-band around the knees is often ineffective for correcting knee valgus.

consequences.text: Knee valgus negatively affects the technical execution and performance of dynamic lifts.
